items.title: I'm the founder of a private jet company. I eat dinner when the locals do and end most days in my at-home bowling alley.
items.summary: VistaJet This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Thomas Flohr, the 65-year-old founder, chairman, and CEO of VistaJet, based in St. Moritz, Switzerland, about his daily routine. It's been edited for length and clarity. I started my career at a Chicago-based technology firm in 1985 and rose through the ranks. I later acquired most of the company's European operations through my company, Comprendium Investment. My frequent business travel in the early 2000s exposed me to the shortcomings of private aviation. At the time, I found the private jet experience to be inconsistent and underwhelming. The service quality didn't match the level of luxury that clients paying $10,000 to $15,000 an hour expected. I didn't see a good solution in the market and initially thought about paying for fractional jet ownership before deciding against it. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. After exploring all other options, I bought a Learjet 60 in 2003, and that plane became the foundation for starting VistaJet in 2004. Vista is a private aviation subscription service that provides access to over 270 customized business jets for clients in 187 countries. My primary job is building client relationships and setting the company's strategic direction. Here's what a typical day in my life looks like. 8 a.m. — Coffee, quiet time, and clearing my inbox Our company is headquartered in Dubai, but I travel frequently and usually work from any of our 25 offices worldwide, including my home office in St. Moritz. I wake up at different times, depending on where I am. If I'm in America, I start earlier to sync with Europe. In the Middle East, I work late into the night to overlap with American and European business hours. In St. Moritz, my mornings start around 8 a.m. I shower, grab coffee, and ease into the day. I don't eat breakfast. I prefer not to reach for my phone right away. About 45 minutes after my coffee, I'll respond to overnight emails and messages before diving into the day's activities. 9 a.m. — Home, office, hotel, or en route I maintain several offices in different locations so my executives can use them when I'm not around. If I'm home, I'll work from my home office. If I'm on the road, I'll work on the plane or at my destination. Sometimes, I work from the hotel in the morning and knock out key business tasks. If I'm in Dubai, London, New York, or a city with a VistaJet office, I'll head there in the afternoon for team and client meetings. I often sit where the action is with the team or join executive committee members in their offices. 10 a.m. — Clients, above all else I prioritize client meetings before internal ones and don't believe internal meetings should take more than 20 to 30 minutes unless there's a compelling reason. When clients call me directly, it's usually because they're about to make a significant decision, like buying a plane or finalizing a global flight plan. I also work on product development, brainstorming new services and product feature updates between calls and meetings. As a founder, I'm still very hands-on, and I'm in constant communication with my finance and operations teams. 12:30 p.m. — Light and simple healthy lunch For lunch, I keep it very light and healthy. I usually eat vegetable soup, a fruit platter, or a light Japanese sashimi dish. If I'm having a client lunch meeting, I prefer to eat at restaurants that use high-quality ingredients. Some of my favorite restaurants include Scott's in Mayfair , London, and Gaia in Dubai. When I eat out, I mostly get grilled seafood and boiled potatoes — nothing fancy. 2 p.m. — Creative solutions to global logistics challenges The afternoon often means syncing with our US and European teams. In our business, there's no shortage of unusual requests that require creative solutions. One memorable request involved helping a client run three marathons on three continents in one week. It was a significant logistical undertaking, but we successfully pulled it off for the client. Another request involved helping a corporate client coordinate the flight of executives from four continents to a board meeting in India, ensuring they all arrived precisely on time and returned home safely afterward. 4:30 p.m. — A brief break to recharge If there's a gap between meetings, I'll take a 10-15-minute break to walk outside and get some fresh air. I try to prioritize these short breaks to clear my head and reset, but most of the time, the day runs nonstop. 6 p.m. — Daily exercise as business preparation By 6 or 6:30 p.m., I head to the gym and spend an hour training. Once I'm done working out, I hit the steam room for 15 to 20 minutes to relax and recover. Staying fit keeps me sharp. I'm a firm believer in an integrated life. I don't view work and life as separate entities that need to be balanced against each other. Instead, I see everything in life as one endurance effort, whether in business or sports like car racing. 8:30 p.m. — Dinner and a little bowling The time I eat dinner varies depending on my location. In some countries, I eat at 7 p.m.; in others, at 9 or 9:30 p.m. I adapt to the time zone and cultural norms. When I'm home, I eat dinner around 8:30 p.m., but I'm always available for client calls if needed. I enjoy cooking and dining with friends and family. I have a bowling alley in my home, so we head downstairs for a few rounds after dinner. It's a great way to unwind and stir up friendly competition. 11 p.m. — Winding down with classical music or late '70s and early '80s rock With so much digital stimulation during the day, I avoid screens at night. I don't watch TV, but I listen to classical music or rock from the late '70s and early '80s before bed. I usually fall asleep around 11:30 p.m., sleeping seven hours on weeknights and nine on weekends. Weekends — Markets and nature Despite flying around 500 hours annually, I make time for things I enjoy. I'm a big fan of simple living and doing things in nature, like walking, hiking, and shopping at my local market for fruits and vegetables. Read the original article on Business Insider

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Thomas Flohr, the 65-year-old founder, chairman, and CEO of VistaJet, based in St. Moritz, Switzerland, about his daily routine. It's been edited for length and clarity.

I started my career at a Chicago-based technology firm in 1985 and rose through the ranks. I later acquired most of the company's European operations through my company, Comprendium Investment.

My frequent business travel in the early 2000s exposed me to the shortcomings of private aviation. At the time, I found the private jet experience to be inconsistent and underwhelming. The service quality didn't match the level of luxury that clients paying $10,000 to $15,000 an hour expected. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine.

After exploring all other options, I bought a Learjet 60 in 2003, and that plane became the foundation for starting VistaJet in 2004. Vista is a private aviation subscription service that provides access to over 270 customized business jets for clients in 187 countries.

My primary job is building client relationships and setting the company's strategic direction. Here's what a typical day in my life looks like.

8 a.m. — Coffee, quiet time, and clearing my inbox

Our company is headquartered in Dubai, but I travel frequently and usually work from any of our 25 offices worldwide, including my home office in St. Moritz. I wake up at different times, depending on where I am. If I'm in America, I start earlier to sync with Europe. In the Middle East, I work late into the night to overlap with American and European business hours.

In St. Moritz, my mornings start around 8 a.m. I shower, grab coffee, and ease into the day. I don't eat breakfast.

I prefer not to reach for my phone right away. About 45 minutes after my coffee, I'll respond to overnight emails and messages before diving into the day's activities.

9 a.m. — Home, office, hotel, or en route

I maintain several offices in different locations so my executives can use them when I'm not around. If I'm home, I'll work from my home office. If I'm on the road, I'll work on the plane or at my destination.

Sometimes, I work from the hotel in the morning and knock out key business tasks. If I'm in Dubai, London, New York, or a city with a VistaJet office, I'll head there in the afternoon for team and client meetings.

I often sit where the action is with the team or join executive committee members in their offices.

10 a.m. — Clients, above all else

I prioritize client meetings before internal ones and don't believe internal meetings should take more than 20 to 30 minutes unless there's a compelling reason.

When clients call me directly, it's usually because they're about to make a significant decision, like buying a plane or finalizing a global flight plan. I also work on product development, brainstorming new services and product feature updates between calls and meetings.

As a founder, I'm still very hands-on, and I'm in constant communication with my finance and operations teams.

12:30 p.m. — Light and simple healthy lunch

For lunch, I keep it very light and healthy. I usually eat vegetable soup, a fruit platter, or a light Japanese sashimi dish.

If I'm having a client lunch meeting, I prefer to eat at restaurants that use high-quality ingredients. Some of my favorite restaurants include Scott's in Mayfair, London, and Gaia in Dubai. When I eat out, I mostly get grilled seafood and boiled potatoes — nothing fancy.

2 p.m. — Creative solutions to global logistics challenges

The afternoon often means syncing with our US and European teams. In our business, there's no shortage of unusual requests that require creative solutions. One memorable request involved helping a client run three marathons on three continents in one week. It was a significant logistical undertaking, but we successfully pulled it off for the client.

Another request involved helping a corporate client coordinate the flight of executives from four continents to a board meeting in India, ensuring they all arrived precisely on time and returned home safely afterward.

4:30 p.m. — A brief break to recharge

If there's a gap between meetings, I'll take a 10-15-minute break to walk outside and get some fresh air. I try to prioritize these short breaks to clear my head and reset, but most of the time, the day runs nonstop.

6 p.m. — Daily exercise as business preparation

By 6 or 6:30 p.m., I head to the gym and spend an hour training. Once I'm done working out, I hit the steam room for 15 to 20 minutes to relax and recover. Staying fit keeps me sharp.

I'm a firm believer in an integrated life. I don't view work and life as separate entities that need to be balanced against each other. Instead, I see everything in life as one endurance effort, whether in business or sports like car racing.

8:30 p.m. — Dinner and a little bowling

The time I eat dinner varies depending on my location. In some countries, I eat at 7 p.m.; in others, at 9 or 9:30 p.m. I adapt to the time zone and cultural norms. When I'm home, I eat dinner around 8:30 p.m., but I'm always available for client calls if needed.

I enjoy cooking and dining with friends and family. I have a bowling alley in my home, so we head downstairs for a few rounds after dinner. It's a great way to unwind and stir up friendly competition.

11 p.m. — Winding down with classical music or late '70s and early '80s rock

With so much digital stimulation during the day, I avoid screens at night. I don't watch TV, but I listen to classical music or rock from the late '70s and early '80s before bed.

I usually fall asleep around 11:30 p.m., sleeping seven hours on weeknights and nine on weekends.

Weekends — Markets and nature

Despite flying around 500 hours annually, I make time for things I enjoy. I'm a big fan of simple living and doing things in nature, like walking, hiking, and shopping at my local market for fruits and vegetables.

items.title: I build AI data centers. I want them to disappear from view.
items.summary: Sean James works at Nvidia as a distinguished engineer. Sean James Sean James is a distinguished engineer at AI chipmaker Nvidia focused on powering data centers. James started his career as a submarine electrician in the Navy and previously spent 25 years building data centers at Microsoft. He makes the case that AI data centers "need to fade into the background" so they're visibly "unremarkable." This first-person essay was written by Sean James , a distinguished engineer in energy systems at Nvidia, where he works on the power and energy infrastructure needed to support AI data centers. He previously spent more than two decades at Microsoft designing and building data centers. Chances are you passed an electrical substation today that delivers power to thousands of homes at hundreds of thousands of volts. It was so unremarkable that you didn't even notice. Sometime in the past, these marvels of engineering simply vanished into the background. For most of my career, when asked, I told people I built data centers . And only in the last five years did people know what one even was. I still don't think my mom knows what I do. Contrast that with today and how often I get calls and see texts asking this and that about data centers. Mostly, it's questions about water usage and energy demand . Data centers went from large concrete buildings assumed to be just another warehouse to headline news. And I want them to disappear again. I recently left Microsoft where I spent 25 years operating, designing, building, and toward the end, innovation. Innovation was all about making data centers less resource intensive, faster to build, and modular so they would come together like Lego bricks. Last month, while cleaning out my home office, I came across a page of notes from 2015. Scrawled across the top: Top 3 Career Goals. One of them read: disappear the data center. This remains the goal. "The most profound technologies are those that disappear." - Mark, Weiser, Scientific American, September 1991. Disappearing tech can still be seen; I am not talking about hiding it. Technology matures until it blends into daily life and stops asking for attention. It becomes unremarkable. Like water mains and substations, infrastructure graduates when it stops being news, stops demanding attention from us. Two decades ago, our focus was to keep data centers invisible by making sure they were always online and powered up and never the source of an outage. Sean James previously spent 25 years designing and building data centers for Microsoft. Sean James Now think of a data center like a factory. An industrial engineer's job is to identify and kill all non-value-added parts. A slug of steel goes in one end, and a wheel comes out the other end, and the mission is to make everything in the middle as elegant, fast, and efficient as possible. The AI factory works the same way, turning electricity into tokens. Unfortunately, data centers are not disappearing today. I would not want to live next to one. Loud, dust, traffic, water, interactions with the grid. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) issued a rare Level 3 alert in May, its highest tier. The trigger: events where more than 1,000 megawatts of data center load dropped off the grid in seconds. Voltage dips are common on the grid, and we don't even notice them in our homes. But data centers are designed to protect their servers. When they sense a dip, they let go of the grid and jump to onsite batteries. The computers ride through without a blink. The grid takes the hit. This type of disappearing makes our grid unstable. Believe me or don't, but I have watched the data center diminish over the decades. Energy needed to cool servers dropped when evaporative cooling replaced chillers. Server companies keep relaxing temperature requirements to make servers easier to cool. PUE, the measure of how energy efficient a data center is, has gone from 3 to 5 in the 90s to 1.2 to 1.5 today. Waste, too. I remember mountains of foam from server packaging. Now racks arrive fully assembled in reusable wooden boxes. Safety at data center projects has become the highest priority. Workers go home whole and projects are uneventful. And those of us who design them are still not satisfied. Chasing the next breakthrough is what gets us out of bed in the morning. Today, the data center is starting to vanish one piece at a time. Nvidia , where I work now, went public this summer with a design that runs coolant at up to 113 degrees, hotter than a hot tub. At that temperature, heat exchangers and outside air can carry the heat away in most climates. No cooling towers. Cooling water use at the site drops to zero. Data centers are also learning to be grid assets instead of liabilities. Grid stabilizers. Flexing to hand capacity back when the grid is stressed. Riding through voltage dips instead of letting go. Even the diesel generators are starting to disappear from the design, replaced by fault-tolerant networks, batteries, and fuel cells. The criticism of data centers is important feedback. A lot of it is accurate. Some of it is not. The encouraging part for me is to see the open dialog. Data center designers can't improve in a vacuum. And the local jurisdictions that set the rules for construction need to modernize them, so that development of any kind meets the needs of the communities that host it. Substations and water towers are critical to modern life. They surround us, quietly hidden in plain sight. Data centers need to fade into the background too, and that is the goal of every data center designer. We will continue to make them efficient, sustainable, and eventually unremarkable. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Why billion-dollar robotics startups are obsessed with folding laundry
items.summary: Weave Robotics' Isaac 1 robot. Weave Robotics Billion-dollar robotics startups are racing to teach robots to fold laundry. Laundry is a safe, contained test for robots entering the chaos of the home, roboticists say. Home robots must learn more chores to justify their steep prices. Before Silicon Valley's robots take over, they have to learn to fold your underwear. In recent months, some of the buzziest robotics startups — including Figure AI , Sunday Robotics, and Weave Robotics — have shown off robots that autonomously fold clothes. Together, the companies have raised billions of dollars at lofty valuations, as investors bet that home robots are finally nearing a commercial breakthrough. We were promised robot butlers. For now, Silicon Valley would like to help you match your socks. Home robotics companies are focusing on laundry because it's an ideal first task. It is difficult enough to showcase a machine's intelligence and physical control, and safe enough that failure carries few consequences, roboticists say. It is also a chore almost everyone does, and few enjoy. Consumers don't need to know how AI works to appreciate a robot that turns a crumpled pile of clothes into a neat stack. Teaching a robot to fold clothing has long been a "holy grail" of the field, said roboticist and Spelman College president Ayanna Howard. That's because robots must learn to handle "deformable objects" — clothes that bunch, fold, and wrinkle — and manipulate them with enough precision to fold them well. Weave Robotics' Isaac 1 robot. Weave Robotics "This is one of the most challenging dexterous manipulation tasks for a humanoid robot," Figure wrote in a blog post last year. Sunday CEO Tony Zhao told Business Insider that the company chose laundry partly because it "looks for hard things to do." Yet when a robot fails, the stakes are low. "If you drop a piece of clothing, it's not going to break," Howard said. The robotics industry has been through laundry hype cycles before. The Japanese company behind the $16,000 laundry-folding robot, Laundroid, filed for bankruptcy in 2019, and FoldiMate made repeated splashes at the Consumer Electronics Show in the late 2010s but never shipped a product. High costs and poor reliability undid those earlier efforts. Today's startups say that advances in AI, cheaper hardware, and a flood of talent and capital into physical AI will make this generation different — and capable of doing far more than laundry. "For the longest time, the technology just wasn't there," Weave Robotics CEO Kaan Dogrusoz told Business Insider. "But then, everything changed." Whether that’s true is about to be tested outside the lab. The latest robots are expensive, and their reliability in real homes remains unknown because few have been deployed. While this generation can fold laundry much faster than its predecessors, a single item can still take minutes to fold, and unfamiliar clothing can leave the machines stumped. Sunday plans to place its robot in homes through a beta program this fall. Weave and 1X expect to begin delivering robots to customers later this year. Why laundry is a gateway into the home Robotics companies are starting with laundry because it's a bounded task inside the home, a tough environment for robots to navigate. "The home is the ultimate unstructured environment," said Matei Ciocarlie, a mechanical engineering professor at Columbia University who works on robotics. Most robots operate in controlled environments such as factories and warehouses , where their surroundings and movements can be tightly defined. They are often separated from people for safety. The home, by comparison, is a hellscape for robots. Every room is an obstacle course. Pets dart underfoot, and toddlers crawl across the floor, threatening to send machines into a faceplant. Sunday Robotics' Memo robot. Sunday Robotics When folding laundry, a robot can stay in one corner while a hamper of clothes is brought to it, rather than having to navigate the entire house. Dogrusoz cited this as the reason Weave chose laundry as the first task. "It's an attempt to put bounds on the craziness," Ciocarlie said. What comes after laundry? Teaching a robot to fold laundry is one thing. Convincing people to pay thousands of dollars for it is another. Weave's Isaac, for instance, costs $8,000 upfront, or $449 a month through a subscription. For most households, it would likely be cheaper to outsource the chore to a laundromat or a person. Or, as Howard put it: "That's what kids are for." For these robots to make economic sense, they need to do far more than fold clothes. Sunday's AI system, for instance, is learning chores including vacuuming, organizing toys, fastening zippers, and making coffee. 1X is marketing its humanoid robot NEO as a personal housekeeper capable of folding laundry, organizing shelves, and tidying rooms. Weave declined to say which task it is tackling next. 1X's NEO humanoid. Camille Cohen for The Washington Post via Getty Images Howard said consumers are unlikely to seriously consider buying a home robot until it can perform enough useful tasks to justify its price, like heating dinner before its owner gets home, mowing the lawn, or cleaning the pool. The challenge will be building a single robot that can do all of these things. Jason Corso, a robotics professor at the University of Michigan, said companies are "stuck in an appliance mindset," building robots around individual chores rather than machines that can understand context and adapt to people's needs. For many of these companies, getting robots into homes to fold laundry is also the start of what they hope will become an expanding data flywheel. Robotics startups are scrambling for real-world data needed to train the "brains" of their machines. While large language models are trained on internet data, there is no comparable dataset for the physical world. Sunday, for example, trains its AI models on people doing everyday tasks in $200 sensor-equipped gloves that mirror its robots' hands. The most valuable data — the kind that could help companies truly master laundry and expand into other tasks — may come from the robots themselves as they encounter the countless edge cases of real homes. A truly general-purpose home robot — the robot butler Silicon Valley has long promised — is still many years away, Corso said. Have a tip? Weave Robotics' Isaac 1 robot.

Weave Robotics

  • Billion-dollar robotics startups are racing to teach robots to fold laundry.
  • Laundry is a safe, contained test for robots entering the chaos of the home, roboticists say.
  • Home robots must learn more chores to justify their steep prices.

Before Silicon Valley's robots take over, they have to learn to fold your underwear.

In recent months, some of the buzziest robotics startups — including Figure AI, Sunday Robotics, and Weave Robotics — have shown off robots that autonomously fold clothes. Together, the companies have raised billions of dollars at lofty valuations, as investors bet that home robots are finally nearing a commercial breakthrough.

We were promised robot butlers. For now, Silicon Valley would like to help you match your socks.

Home robotics companies are focusing on laundry because it's an ideal first task. It is difficult enough to showcase a machine's intelligence and physical control, and safe enough that failure carries few consequences, roboticists say. It is also a chore almost everyone does, and few enjoy. Consumers don't need to know how AI works to appreciate a robot that turns a crumpled pile of clothes into a neat stack.

Teaching a robot to fold clothing has long been a "holy grail" of the field, said roboticist and Spelman College president Ayanna Howard. That's because robots must learn to handle "deformable objects" — clothes that bunch, fold, and wrinkle — and manipulate them with enough precision to fold them well.

Weave Robotics' Isaac 1 robot.

Weave Robotics

"This is one of the most challenging dexterous manipulation tasks for a humanoid robot," Figure wrote in a blog post last year. Sunday CEO Tony Zhao told Business Insider that the company chose laundry partly because it "looks for hard things to do."

Yet when a robot fails, the stakes are low.

"If you drop a piece of clothing, it's not going to break," Howard said.

The robotics industry has been through laundry hype cycles before. The Japanese company behind the $16,000 laundry-folding robot, Laundroid, filed for bankruptcy in 2019, and FoldiMate made repeated splashes at the Consumer Electronics Show in the late 2010s but never shipped a product.

High costs and poor reliability undid those earlier efforts. Today's startups say that advances in AI, cheaper hardware, and a flood of talent and capital into physical AI will make this generation different — and capable of doing far more than laundry.

"For the longest time, the technology just wasn't there," Weave Robotics CEO Kaan Dogrusoz told Business Insider. "But then, everything changed."

Whether that’s true is about to be tested outside the lab. The latest robots are expensive, and their reliability in real homes remains unknown because few have been deployed. While this generation can fold laundry much faster than its predecessors, a single item can still take minutes to fold, and unfamiliar clothing can leave the machines stumped.

Sunday plans to place its robot in homes through a beta program this fall. Weave and 1X expect to begin delivering robots to customers later this year.

Why laundry is a gateway into the home

Robotics companies are starting with laundry because it's a bounded task inside the home, a tough environment for robots to navigate.

"The home is the ultimate unstructured environment," said Matei Ciocarlie, a mechanical engineering professor at Columbia University who works on robotics.

Most robots operate in controlled environments such as factories and warehouses, where their surroundings and movements can be tightly defined. They are often separated from people for safety.

The home, by comparison, is a hellscape for robots. Every room is an obstacle course. Pets dart underfoot, and toddlers crawl across the floor, threatening to send machines into a faceplant.

Sunday Robotics' Memo robot.

Sunday Robotics

When folding laundry, a robot can stay in one corner while a hamper of clothes is brought to it, rather than having to navigate the entire house. Dogrusoz cited this as the reason Weave chose laundry as the first task.

"It's an attempt to put bounds on the craziness," Ciocarlie said.

What comes after laundry?

Teaching a robot to fold laundry is one thing. Convincing people to pay thousands of dollars for it is another.

Weave's Isaac, for instance, costs $8,000 upfront, or $449 a month through a subscription. For most households, it would likely be cheaper to outsource the chore to a laundromat or a person. Or, as Howard put it: "That's what kids are for."

For these robots to make economic sense, they need to do far more than fold clothes.

Sunday's AI system, for instance, is learning chores including vacuuming, organizing toys, fastening zippers, and making coffee. 1X is marketing its humanoid robot NEO as a personal housekeeper capable of folding laundry, organizing shelves, and tidying rooms. Weave declined to say which task it is tackling next.

1X's NEO humanoid.

Camille Cohen for The Washington Post via Getty Images

Howard said consumers are unlikely to seriously consider buying a home robot until it can perform enough useful tasks to justify its price, like heating dinner before its owner gets home, mowing the lawn, or cleaning the pool. The challenge will be building a single robot that can do all of these things.

Jason Corso, a robotics professor at the University of Michigan, said companies are "stuck in an appliance mindset," building robots around individual chores rather than machines that can understand context and adapt to people's needs.

For many of these companies, getting robots into homes to fold laundry is also the start of what they hope will become an expanding data flywheel. Robotics startups are scrambling for real-world data needed to train the "brains" of their machines. While large language models are trained on internet data, there is no comparable dataset for the physical world. Sunday, for example, trains its AI models on people doing everyday tasks in $200 sensor-equipped gloves that mirror its robots' hands.

The most valuable data — the kind that could help companies truly master laundry and expand into other tasks — may come from the robots themselves as they encounter the countless edge cases of real homes.

A truly general-purpose home robot — the robot butler Silicon Valley has long promised — is still many years away, Corso said.

items.title: Google dismantles Deepmind and bets on a fresh start as Hassabis heads for the exit
items.summary: Google Deepmind is losing its autonomy, and founder Demis Hassabis may leave the AI lab for good in the coming months. AI researcher Koray Kavukcuoglu will take over day-to-day operations without the CEO title, and all Gemini development is moving to the Bay Area. Internally, Google is apparently struggling with serious problems training frontier models, even as its cloud business generates billions. The question is whether the company is deliberately betting on infrastructure or simply can't catch the leaders. The article Google dismantles Deepmind and bets on a fresh start as Hassabis heads for the exit appeared first on The Decoder .

items.title: AVCaptureMultiCamSession: the real limits, and why the stock Camera app doesn't offer dual recording
items.summary:
Modern iPhones can genuinely run the front and back cameras at the same time. AVCaptureMultiCamSession has been in the SDK since iOS 13 and works on A12 and later hardware. And yet Apple's own Camera app has no dual-recording mode, no toggle, no hidden gesture. That is not a product oversight you can route around. iOS has two separate concepts: a normal AVCaptureSession runs exactly one camera and can switch between them, and a multi-camera session runs several inputs concurrently. The second is a different object with different rules, and almost everything you know about the first one is wrong for it. Here is what those rules actually cost, from a shipping dual-camera recorder. The problem You want one MP4 containing both cameras, composited live, with a preview that matches the file. The pieces sound routine: two inputs, two outputs, a compositor, an AVAssetWriter . Why the obvious approach fails addInput / addOutput simply fail The convenience API implicitly forms connections for you. On a multi-cam session that fails outright. You must add inputs and outputs without connections and wire AVCaptureConnection objects yourself: private func addVideoBranch ( device : AVCaptureDevice , output : AVCaptureVideoDataOutput , mirrored : Bool ) throws { let input = try AVCaptureDeviceInput ( device : device ) guard session . canAddInput ( input ) else { throw ConfigError . cannotAdd ( " \( device . position ) input" ) } session . addInputWithNoConnections ( input ) output . videoSettings = [ kCVPixelBufferPixelFormatTypeKey as String : kCVPixelFormatType_32BGRA ] output . alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames = true guard session . canAddOutput ( output ) else { throw ConfigError . cannotAdd ( " \( device . position ) output" ) } session . addOutputWithNoConnections ( output ) guard let port = input . ports ( for : . video , sourceDeviceType : device . deviceType , sourceDevicePosition : device . position ) . first else { throw ConfigError . noPort ( " \( device . position ) " ) } let conn = AVCaptureConnection ( inputPorts : [ port ], output : output ) guard session . canAddConnection ( conn ) else { throw ConfigError . cannotAdd ( " \( device . position ) connection" ) } session . addConnection ( conn ) if conn . isVideoRotationAngleSupported ( 90 ) { conn . videoRotationAngle = 90 } if mirrored , conn . isVideoMirroringSupported { conn . automaticallyAdjustsVideoMirroring = false conn . isVideoMirrored = true } } sessionPreset does not work either A multi-cam session only accepts .inputPriority . Resolution is chosen per device by picking an activeFormat , only from formats where isMultiCamSupported == true — and it must be chosen before addInput : private func configureFormat ( for device : AVCaptureDevice , targetWidth : Int32 ) throws { let multiCamFormats = device . formats . filter { $0 . isMultiCamSupported } guard ! multiCamFormats . isEmpty else { throw ConfigError . noFormat ( " \( device . position ) " ) } func supports30fps ( _ f : AVCaptureDevice . Format ) -> Bool { f . videoSupportedFrameRateRanges . contains { $0 . minFrameRate <= 30 && $0 . maxFrameRate >= 30 } } func dims ( _ f : AVCaptureDevice . Format ) -> CMVideoDimensions { CMVideoFormatDescriptionGetDimensions ( f . formatDescription ) } let chosen = multiCamFormats . first ( where : { dims ( $0 ) . width == targetWidth && supports30fps ( $0 ) }) ?? multiCamFormats . max ( by : { a , b in Int ( dims ( a ) . width ) * Int ( dims ( a ) . height ) < Int ( dims ( b ) . width ) * Int ( dims ( b ) . height ) }) ! try device . lockForConfiguration () defer { device . unlockForConfiguration () } device . activeFormat = chosen let duration = CMTime ( value : 1 , timescale : 30 ) device . activeVideoMinFrameDuration = duration device . activeVideoMaxFrameDuration = duration } Note filter { $0.isMultiCamSupported } . The set of multi-cam formats is a strict subset of what the device offers when it is the only camera running. This is the first place the "why not just do what the Camera app does" answer starts to appear: the Camera app is not choosing from the same menu. The hardwareCost gate — and it cannot be pre-checked This is the constraint that shapes the whole feature. A multi-cam configuration has a hardwareCost and a systemPressureCost . If hardwareCost > 1.0 you get a runtime error and the session dies. And the value only reflects the new configuration after you commit it . There is no dry run. So every configuration change has to be: change → commit → read cost → roll back if over. session . beginConfiguration () do { try configureFormat ( for : back , targetWidth : r . targetWidth ) try configureFormat ( for : front , targetWidth : r . targetWidth ) } catch { session . commitConfiguration () errorMessage = L10n . Error . detail ( Strings . resolutionFailed , error . localizedDescription ) await startSession () return } session . commitConfiguration () if session . hardwareCost > 1.0 { downgraded = true applied = previous session . beginConfiguration () try ? configureFormat ( for : back , targetWidth : previous . targetWidth ) try ? configureFormat ( for : front , targetWidth : previous . targetWidth ) session . commitConfiguration () } Dual 1080p exceeds the budget easily on many devices. That rollback is not defensive tidiness — remove it and you ship an app that dies when a user picks a resolution their phone cannot sustain. The seamless zoom is not available to you The stock Camera app's continuous pinch from ultra-wide through wide to telephoto is built on a virtual capture device that internally owns several physical lenses and crossfades between them. A multi-cam session connects to specific physical devices, because that is what the isMultiCamSupported format check operates on. A virtual device that silently reaches across several lenses is not something that check can reason about. The consequence for the UI is that lens choice and zoom become two different controls, and the lens picker may list fewer lenses than the stock app shows: /// Running three back lenses at once under MultiCam is impossible and unnecessary — /// probe only which lenses have a multicam format, then use the chosen one as the /// single back input. private func discoverBackLenses () { var found : [ BackLens ] = [] for lens in BackLens . allCases { guard let device = Self . device ( for : lens ) else { continue } guard device . formats . contains ( where : { $0 . isMultiCamSupported }) else { continue } found . append ( lens ) } availableBackLenses = found if ! found . contains ( backLens ) { backLens = found . contains ( . wide ) ? . wide : ( found . first ?? . wide ) } } Front camera zoom, incidentally, is 1.0 and stays 1.0: there is no optical zoom there, so videoMaxZoomFactor is 1. If the front camera is your main frame, pinch-to-zoom does nothing, and the honest move is to say so rather than let a gesture look broken. What actually works One clock, one texture Two camera streams do not arrive in lockstep. The design that avoids an entire class of bugs is to treat one camera as the clock and hold only the latest frame from the other, then render one texture that is used for both the preview and the writer: func captureOutput ( _ output : AVCaptureOutput , didOutput sampleBuffer : CMSampleBuffer , from connection : AVCaptureConnection ) { if output is AVCaptureAudioDataOutput { if recorder . isRecording { recorder . appendAudio ( sampleBuffer ) } return } guard let pixelBuffer = CMSampleBufferGetImageBuffer ( sampleBuffer ) else { return } guard isBack ( output ) else { latestFront = pixelBuffer // front camera: keep only the newest frame return } // the back camera is the clock guard let front = latestFront else { return } let pool : CVPixelBufferPool ? = recorder . isRecording ? recorder . pixelBufferPool : nil if let composed = compositor . render ( back : pixelBuffer , front : front , recordingPool : pool ) { recorder . appendVideo ( composed , pts : CMSampleBufferGetPresentationTimeStamp ( sampleBuffer )) } } The composite is rendered directly into a buffer taken from the asset writer's pixelBufferPool , and that texture is then sampled to the screen. Preview and recording are structurally incapable of disagreeing. Splitting this into two independent render paths as an "optimisation" reintroduces the worst bug class in this domain: looks right on screen, wrong in the file. All three outputs share one serial data queue and never touch the main actor. Treat resilience as four named failure paths Four things end a dual recording, and each one destroys the file if unhandled: path consequence if ignored session interrupted (call, another app takes the camera) AVAssetWriter stuck half-open, corrupt file mediaServicesWereReset reusing old inputs/outputs silently stops delivering frames — no error, the picture just freezes thermal state reaches .critical the system kills the session; the whole in-progress take is lost storage fills writer fails outright, entire recording lost The mediaServicesWereReset one is the nastiest because there is no error at all — you must rebuild the whole session. And all automatic stops must funnel through the same finalize path the user's own stop button uses. A second teardown path is how you get one code path that saves the file and another that doesn't. The thermal and storage policies are pure functions, which is the only way they get tested: enum CapturePolicy { static let videoBitrate : Int = 10_000_000 static let minBytesToStart : Int64 = 200 * 1024 * 1024 static let minBytesToContinue : Int64 = 100 * 1024 * 1024 static func thermalAction ( level : ThermalLevel , isRecording : Bool , isHD1080 : Bool ) -> ThermalAction { switch level { case . critical : return isRecording ? . stopRecording : . none case . serious : if ! isRecording , isHD1080 { return . dropTo720 } return . none case . nominal , . fair : return . none } } } The asymmetry is deliberate: at serious , drop to 720p only if you have not started yet — starting a heavy take on an already-hot phone is how you get an interrupted one — but if you are already recording, warn rather than yank the resolution mid-file. Focus coordinates, the silent inversion focusPointOfInterest is expressed in the unrotated landscape sensor frame . It does not follow videoRotationAngle or isVideoMirrored . Converting from a normalised portrait canvas point: back camera (rotation 90): (u, v) = (y, 1 - x) front camera (rotation 90 + mirrored): (u, v) = (y, x) Get it backwards and nothing crashes and nothing logs. Tapping the top-left just focuses the bottom-right. This is why that conversion is a pure function with dozens of tests — and those tests were mutation-verified: swapping the front/back formulas makes them fail immediately. There is still a hole worth being honest about. The tests lock the contract of the pure function, and the contract assumes both connections set videoRotationAngle = 90 with the front additionally mirrored. Change those two lines in the session and every test stays green while focus is inverted on a real phone. Costs and boundaries Nothing camera-related can be verified in the simulator. AVCaptureMultiCamSession.isMultiCamSupported is permanently false there, so
the app correctly shows an unsupported-device screen. Every capture change needs
a real A12-or-later device. (Do not hardcode a model list — that system flag is
the only authority. Apple documents A12+, which is where "iPhone XS/XR or newer"
comes from, but the flag is what you branch on.) Heat and battery are materially worse than single-camera recording. Two
sensors, two ISP paths, a Metal composite per frame and an encoder. Users notice. Layout crops. Side-by-side portrait means fitting a 720×1280 source into a
540×1920 column — 25% is lost from each side. That is arithmetic, not a bug, but
it must be designed around. Some things get frozen at record time. Muting is implemented by not creating
an audio track at start() , which is more robust than writing a silent track, so
it cannot be toggled mid-recording. Aspect ratio likewise cannot change during a
take without destroying the writer. Metal has its own traps here. half is a builtin type name and cannot be a
variable (the compiler error is wildly misleading); multiple draw calls must use setVertexBytes / setFragmentBytes rather than sharing one MTLBuffer at
offset 0; and CVMetalTexture objects must be kept alive until the command
buffer completes. iOS 17+ blocks the easy device screenshot path , so visual verification of a
camera app is manual. Plan for it. This is the capture stack behind DualCam, an iOS app that records both cameras into a single composited file.
items.summary_html:
Modern iPhones can genuinely run the front and back cameras at the same time.
AVCaptureMultiCamSession has been in the SDK since iOS 13 and works on A12 and
later hardware. And yet Apple's own Camera app has no dual-recording mode, no
toggle, no hidden gesture.

That is not a product oversight you can route around. iOS has two separate
concepts: a normal AVCaptureSession runs exactly one camera and can switch
between them, and a multi-camera session runs several inputs concurrently. The
second is a different object with different rules, and almost everything you know
about the first one is wrong for it.

Here is what those rules actually cost, from a shipping dual-camera recorder.

The problem

You want one MP4 containing both cameras, composited live, with a preview that
matches the file. The pieces sound routine: two inputs, two outputs, a compositor,
an AVAssetWriter.

Why the obvious approach fails addInput / addOutput simply fail

The convenience API implicitly forms connections for you. On a multi-cam session
that fails outright. You must add inputs and outputs without connections and wire
AVCaptureConnection objects yourself:

private func addVideoBranch(device: AVCaptureDevice,
                            output: AVCaptureVideoDataOutput,
                            mirrored: Bool) throws {
    let input = try AVCaptureDeviceInput(device: device)
    guard session.canAddInput(input) else { throw ConfigError.cannotAdd("\(device.position) input") }
    session.addInputWithNoConnections(input)

    output.videoSettings = [kCVPixelBufferPixelFormatTypeKey as String: kCVPixelFormatType_32BGRA]
    output.alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames = true
    guard session.canAddOutput(output) else { throw ConfigError.cannotAdd("\(device.position) output") }
    session.addOutputWithNoConnections(output)

    guard let port = input.ports(for: .video,
                                 sourceDeviceType: device.deviceType,
                                 sourceDevicePosition: device.position).first else {
        throw ConfigError.noPort("\(device.position)")
    }

    let conn = AVCaptureConnection(inputPorts: [port], output: output)
    guard session.canAddConnection(conn) else { throw ConfigError.cannotAdd("\(device.position) connection") }
    session.addConnection(conn)

    if conn.isVideoRotationAngleSupported(90) { conn.videoRotationAngle = 90 }
    if mirrored, conn.isVideoMirroringSupported {
        conn.automaticallyAdjustsVideoMirroring = false
        conn.isVideoMirrored = true
    }
}
sessionPreset does not work either

A multi-cam session only accepts .inputPriority. Resolution is chosen per device
by picking an activeFormat, only from formats where isMultiCamSupported == true
— and it must be chosen before addInput:

private func configureFormat(for device: AVCaptureDevice, targetWidth: Int32) throws {
    let multiCamFormats = device.formats.filter { $0.isMultiCamSupported }
    guard !multiCamFormats.isEmpty else { throw ConfigError.noFormat("\(device.position)") }

    func supports30fps(_ f: AVCaptureDevice.Format) -> Bool {
        f.videoSupportedFrameRateRanges.contains { $0.minFrameRate <= 30 && $0.maxFrameRate >= 30 }
    }
    func dims(_ f: AVCaptureDevice.Format) -> CMVideoDimensions {
        CMVideoFormatDescriptionGetDimensions(f.formatDescription)
    }

    let chosen = multiCamFormats.first(where: { dims($0).width == targetWidth && supports30fps($0) })
        ?? multiCamFormats.max(by: { a, b in
            Int(dims(a).width) * Int(dims(a).height) < Int(dims(b).width) * Int(dims(b).height)
        })!

    try device.lockForConfiguration()
    defer { device.unlockForConfiguration() }
    device.activeFormat = chosen
    let duration = CMTime(value: 1, timescale: 30)
    device.activeVideoMinFrameDuration = duration
    device.activeVideoMaxFrameDuration = duration
}

Note filter { $0.isMultiCamSupported }. The set of multi-cam formats is a strict
subset of what the device offers when it is the only camera running. This is the
first place the "why not just do what the Camera app does" answer starts to appear:
the Camera app is not choosing from the same menu.

The hardwareCost gate — and it cannot be pre-checked

This is the constraint that shapes the whole feature. A multi-cam configuration has
a hardwareCost and a systemPressureCost. If hardwareCost > 1.0 you get a
runtime error and the session dies. And the value only reflects the new
configuration after you commit it. There is no dry run.

So every configuration change has to be: change → commit → read cost → roll back if
over.

session.beginConfiguration()
do {
    try configureFormat(for: back,  targetWidth: r.targetWidth)
    try configureFormat(for: front, targetWidth: r.targetWidth)
} catch {
    session.commitConfiguration()
    errorMessage = L10n.Error.detail(Strings.resolutionFailed, error.localizedDescription)
    await startSession()
    return
}
session.commitConfiguration()

if session.hardwareCost > 1.0 {
    downgraded = true
    applied = previous
    session.beginConfiguration()
    try? configureFormat(for: back,  targetWidth: previous.targetWidth)
    try? configureFormat(for: front, targetWidth: previous.targetWidth)
    session.commitConfiguration()
}

Dual 1080p exceeds the budget easily on many devices. That rollback is not
defensive tidiness — remove it and you ship an app that dies when a user picks a
resolution their phone cannot sustain.

The seamless zoom is not available to you

The stock Camera app's continuous pinch from ultra-wide through wide to telephoto
is built on a virtual capture device that internally owns several physical lenses
and crossfades between them. A multi-cam session connects to specific physical
devices, because that is what the isMultiCamSupported format check operates on. A
virtual device that silently reaches across several lenses is not something that
check can reason about.

The consequence for the UI is that lens choice and zoom become two different
controls, and the lens picker may list fewer lenses than the stock app shows:

/// Running three back lenses at once under MultiCam is impossible and unnecessary —
/// probe only which lenses have a multicam format, then use the chosen one as the
/// single back input.
private func discoverBackLenses() {
    var found: [BackLens] = []
    for lens in BackLens.allCases {
        guard let device = Self.device(for: lens) else { continue }
        guard device.formats.contains(where: { $0.isMultiCamSupported }) else { continue }
        found.append(lens)
    }
    availableBackLenses = found
    if !found.contains(backLens) {
        backLens = found.contains(.wide) ? .wide : (found.first ?? .wide)
    }
}

Front camera zoom, incidentally, is 1.0 and stays 1.0: there is no optical zoom
there, so videoMaxZoomFactor is 1. If the front camera is your main frame,
pinch-to-zoom does nothing, and the honest move is to say so rather than let a
gesture look broken.

What actually works One clock, one texture

Two camera streams do not arrive in lockstep. The design that avoids an entire
class of bugs is to treat one camera as the clock and hold only the latest frame
from the other, then render one texture that is used for both the preview and
the writer:

func captureOutput(_ output: AVCaptureOutput,
                   didOutput sampleBuffer: CMSampleBuffer,
                   from connection: AVCaptureConnection) {

    if output is AVCaptureAudioDataOutput {
        if recorder.isRecording { recorder.appendAudio(sampleBuffer) }
        return
    }

    guard let pixelBuffer = CMSampleBufferGetImageBuffer(sampleBuffer) else { return }

    guard isBack(output) else {
        latestFront = pixelBuffer   // front camera: keep only the newest frame
        return
    }

    // the back camera is the clock
    guard let front = latestFront else { return }

    let pool: CVPixelBufferPool? = recorder.isRecording ? recorder.pixelBufferPool : nil
    if let composed = compositor.render(back: pixelBuffer, front: front, recordingPool: pool) {
        recorder.appendVideo(composed, pts: CMSampleBufferGetPresentationTimeStamp(sampleBuffer))
    }
}

The composite is rendered directly into a buffer taken from the asset writer's
pixelBufferPool, and that texture is then sampled to the screen. Preview and
recording are structurally incapable of disagreeing. Splitting this into two
independent render paths as an "optimisation" reintroduces the worst bug class in
this domain: looks right on screen, wrong in the file.

All three outputs share one serial data queue and never touch the main actor.

Treat resilience as four named failure paths

Four things end a dual recording, and each one destroys the file if unhandled:

path consequence if ignored session interrupted (call, another app takes the camera) AVAssetWriter stuck half-open, corrupt file mediaServicesWereReset reusing old inputs/outputs silently stops delivering frames — no error, the picture just freezes thermal state reaches .critical the system kills the session; the whole in-progress take is lost storage fills writer fails outright, entire recording lost

The mediaServicesWereReset one is the nastiest because there is no error at all —
you must rebuild the whole session. And all automatic stops must funnel through the
same finalize path the user's own stop button uses. A second teardown path is how
you get one code path that saves the file and another that doesn't.

The thermal and storage policies are pure functions, which is the only way they get
tested:

enum CapturePolicy {
    static let videoBitrate: Int = 10_000_000
    static let minBytesToStart: Int64 = 200 * 1024 * 1024
    static let minBytesToContinue: Int64 = 100 * 1024 * 1024

    static func thermalAction(level: ThermalLevel, isRecording: Bool, isHD1080: Bool) -> ThermalAction {
        switch level {
        case .critical:
            return isRecording ? .stopRecording : .none
        case .serious:
            if !isRecording, isHD1080 { return .dropTo720 }
            return .none
        case .nominal, .fair:
            return .none
        }
    }
}

The asymmetry is deliberate: at serious, drop to 720p only if you have not
started yet — starting a heavy take on an already-hot phone is how you get an
interrupted one — but if you are already recording, warn rather than yank the
resolution mid-file.

Focus coordinates, the silent inversion

focusPointOfInterest is expressed in the unrotated landscape sensor frame. It
does not follow videoRotationAngle or isVideoMirrored. Converting from a
normalised portrait canvas point:

  • back camera (rotation 90): (u, v) = (y, 1 - x)
  • front camera (rotation 90 + mirrored): (u, v) = (y, x)

Get it backwards and nothing crashes and nothing logs. Tapping the top-left just
focuses the bottom-right. This is why that conversion is a pure function with
dozens of tests — and those tests were mutation-verified: swapping the front/back
formulas makes them fail immediately.

There is still a hole worth being honest about. The tests lock the contract of the
pure function, and the contract assumes both connections set
videoRotationAngle = 90 with the front additionally mirrored. Change those two
lines in the session and every test stays green while focus is inverted on a real
phone.

Costs and boundaries
  • Nothing camera-related can be verified in the simulator. AVCaptureMultiCamSession.isMultiCamSupported is permanently false there, so the app correctly shows an unsupported-device screen. Every capture change needs a real A12-or-later device. (Do not hardcode a model list — that system flag is the only authority. Apple documents A12+, which is where "iPhone XS/XR or newer" comes from, but the flag is what you branch on.)
  • Heat and battery are materially worse than single-camera recording. Two sensors, two ISP paths, a Metal composite per frame and an encoder. Users notice.
  • Layout crops. Side-by-side portrait means fitting a 720×1280 source into a 540×1920 column — 25% is lost from each side. That is arithmetic, not a bug, but it must be designed around.
  • Some things get frozen at record time. Muting is implemented by not creating an audio track at start(), which is more robust than writing a silent track, so it cannot be toggled mid-recording. Aspect ratio likewise cannot change during a take without destroying the writer.
  • Metal has its own traps here. half is a builtin type name and cannot be a variable (the compiler error is wildly misleading); multiple draw calls must use setVertexBytes/setFragmentBytes rather than sharing one MTLBuffer at offset 0; and CVMetalTexture objects must be kept alive until the command buffer completes.
  • iOS 17+ blocks the easy device screenshot path, so visual verification of a camera app is manual. Plan for it.

This is the capture stack behind DualCam, an iOS app that records both cameras into
a single composited file.
